title: Throwing a porcelain wall pocket vase
subtitle: A vase thrown in porcelain and altered while leather-hard to flatten the back for wall mounting, with two hanging holes pierced above the shoulder
excerpt: A wall pocket vase holds a few cut stems or a small succulent on a wall, flat-backed so it sits flush against the surface. The piece is thrown as a closed or nearly-closed form in porcelain, then altered at the leather-hard stage: the back wall is gently pressed flat from the inside and two small holes are pierced near the top for cord hanging. Porcelain at this scale is demanding: the clay is less forgiving than stoneware, and altering a thrown form without distorting the front profile requires patience and dry hands.
sourceNotes: Wall pocket vase throwing and altering pattern derived from first principles. Flat-backed vase form documented in V&A open-access collection and in early twentieth-century art pottery studio accounts. Porcelain altering technique from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: The working stage where clay holds its shape but remains firm enough to alter without collapsing and damp enough to smooth the altered surface
Air-dried but unfired; porcelain at bone-dry is particularly fragile and should be handled with care
Wrapping both hands around a cylinder and squeezing inward while the wheel turns, to narrow the form and build height without pulling
The first firing, around cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius), that hardens greenware into porous bisqueware
The point during firing at which clay particles fuse into a glass-like, non-porous mass. Porcelain at cone 10 is fully vitrified and translucent in thin sections.

content.text: A wall pocket vase is a small closed form that hangs flat against a wall and holds a few stems or a trailing plant. It is thrown in porcelain as a nearly closed vase form, then altered at the
leather-hard

stage: the back wall is pressed gently flat from the inside using a paddle or flat rib, and two small holes are pierced near the shoulder for hanging cord. The front retains the rounded thrown profile; the flat back allows it to sit flush against the wall.

This is an advanced project because porcelain is less plastic and more prone to cracking than stoneware, particularly during the altering stage. Porcelain does not forgive rushed centring, uneven walls, or over-wetted clay. The reward is a translucent finish quality after
vitrification
that stoneware cannot match.

attrs.title: Studio safety
attrs.content: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no compressed air, no dry sanding indoors. Ventilation matters: a downdraft vent or open window with an extractor. Wear welder's shade-5 glasses when peephole-watching at high temperatures. Never open a hot kiln below 80 degrees Celsius. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach.

content.text: What you'll need
Preparation

Wedge 350 g of porcelain with a gentle spiral or ram's head technique: porcelain wedges differently from stoneware and tears if overworked. It should be smooth and homogeneous with no visible cracks or air bubbles. Keep your hands lightly moist rather than wet during throwing: porcelain absorbs water faster than stoneware and becomes oversaturated and floppy if worked too wet. Have a clean wooden paddle or the flat of a wooden rib to hand for the flattening step at leather-hard. Plan the total form height: the finished vase will be approximately 16 cm tall and 10 cm in maximum diameter before altering. Fix a bat to the wheel head.
Throwing
Centre 350 g of porcelain at medium speed. Porcelain is denser and less grippy than stoneware: use steady, even pressure and take your time. Do not proceed until the clay is completely centred.
Open a floor 50 mm in diameter, leaving 7 mm of clay at the base. Keep the opening narrow: this is a vase form, not a bowl.

Pull the walls upward in three passes. Aim for an even wall of 4 to 5 mm. Porcelain at this weight will pull cleanly to a good height: 14 to 16 cm. Keep the cylinder slightly inward-tapering to prevent the walls from splaying.

Throw a nearly closed vase form in porcelain. Leave it to reach leather-hard. Press the back wall gently flat using a paddle or flat rib. Pierce two small holes near the shoulder. Thread a cord through the holes to hang the vase on a wall. The front stays round. The flat back sits flush against the wall.
Narrow the upper third by
collaring

: wrap both hands around the neck and squeeze inward gently as the wheel turns slowly. Work up from 80 mm diameter at the shoulder to 30 mm at the neck in two passes. The neck opening should be 30 mm in diameter, enough to insert a small stem or a small glass water tube.

Refine the profile with the metal rib held against the belly of the form. The outside surface of porcelain smooths beautifully with a metal rib but the tool pressure must be very light: too much pressure on a narrow neck will distort the form.
Smooth and compress the rim of the neck with the chamois leather or a wetted finger. Wire off and leave on the bat, covered loosely, to dry to leather-hard before altering.
Altering the back and piercing the hanging holes

When the vase has reached leather-hard, hold it firmly with both hands and gently press the back wall inward with the heel of one hand from the outside. The belly of the vase has enough clay to absorb the flattening without cracking. Work slowly: push in 10 mm at a time, then rotate the vase and check the front profile. The goal is a flat back face approximately 60 mm wide, while the front retains its rounded thrown curve.

If the back wall wrinkles or cracks slightly during pressing, smooth the inside with a finger through the neck opening using the throwing stick handle as an extension. Work from the inside to push the wall back out slightly and smooth the wrinkle. Do not try to press further: accept the flatness achieved in one session.

Place the vase on a banding wheel and check that it sits stable with the flat back down. The flat back will now be the hanging face. Use the calipers to mark two points on the flat back face, each 20 mm in from the side edge and 15 mm down from the shoulder curve.

Pierce the two hanging holes with the needle tool: hold the needle at 90 degrees to the flat face and rotate it gently to bore a clean 4 mm hole at each marked point. Smooth the hole edges inside and out with a wetted finger. Allow the vase to return to leather-hard firmness before trimming.
Trimming

Invert the vase onto the wheel head, centering on its now-altered base footprint. The base may no longer be perfectly round after altering: centre the vase on its widest axis. Porcelain trims cleanly with a sharp loop tool.

Trim the base of the vase to a small circular foot ring, approximately 40 mm in diameter. The foot ring is decorative rather than functional since the vase will hang, but it gives the base a finished look and reduces the area of clay that must stay clear of glaze.

Smooth the foot ring edges carefully. Porcelain at leather-hard trims extremely cleanly but chips at the foot ring edges more readily than stoneware: keep the loop tool sharp and the clay at the right moisture level.
Drying
Dry the altered vase upright, flat back toward a wall so the altered face does not distort under gravity. Cover loosely with light plastic for the first 24 hours. Porcelain at
bone-dry
is significantly more fragile than stoneware at the same stage: do not stack, clatter, or drop the piece. Handle only by supporting the base.
Bisque firing
Load the bone-dry vase upright on a kiln shelf. Place it front-face down if the flat back is stable, or upright if the base sits level.
Bisque

fire to cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius) with a slow moisture-drive ramp: 40 degrees Celsius per hour to 150 degrees Celsius, then 100 degrees Celsius per hour to cone 06. Porcelain bisqueware is still fragile: handle with care after firing.
Glazing and glaze firing

A transparent or celadon glaze suits porcelain's translucent quality. Pour glaze into the vase neck, swirl and pour out to coat the interior. Dip-glaze the exterior. Leave the foot ring and 4 mm of the base unglazed. Leave the two hanging holes clear: insert a cocktail stick into each hole after glazing to keep them open if glaze runs in. Wipe the flat back face to a thin coat so the flat plane reads as a distinct surface. Glaze-fire to cone 10 (1285 degrees Celsius). At cone 10 the porcelain reaches full
vitrification
and the glaze fuses completely. Use a slow final ramp above 1150 degrees Celsius.
Care

Fully fired porcelain is non-porous and does not require sealing. The hanging holes accept a length of waxed linen cord, jute, or thin leather. Thread a 40 cm length through both holes and knot below the flat face; the knot bears the weight. Do not fill the vase with water beyond the neck: the flat-back form will not hold the additional weight evenly when hung. Use a small glass test tube inserted into the neck as a water container for cut stems.
Variations

For a more architectural form, throw the vase as a straight-sided cylinder rather than a bellied vase. Alter the back flat and pierce two hanging holes in the same position. The cylinder version holds a single large stem dramatically against a pale wall.
A set of three wall pocket vases at different scales from the same porcelain batch makes a grouped wall installation. Throw at 350 g, 250 g, and 180 g respectively and hang at staggered heights.

For a textured exterior, roll the thrown form lightly against a piece of coarse-weave fabric or a textured roller at the leather-hard stage before pressing the back flat. The impressed texture survives the altering and glaze firing to give a surface contrast against the smooth glaze coat.

rows.cause: Clay too wet or collaring applied too forcefully
rows.fix: Allow the thrown form to stiffen slightly before collaring: 10 minutes under a slow fan or in a dry room. Collar with two gentle passes rather than one aggressive squeeze.

rows.problem: Back face cracks when pressed flat
rows.cause: Clay too dry at the altering stage, or pressed too far too quickly
rows.fix: Alter when the clay is at true leather-hard, not past it. Press the back in 10 mm per session; if cracks appear, stop and let the vase dry a little more before trying to smooth the crack from inside.

rows.problem: Hanging holes crack or close during drying
rows.cause: Clay shrinkage closed the pierced hole, or the hole was pierced too close to the shoulder curve
rows.fix: Pierce the holes 5 mm larger than the target diameter (porcelain shrinks approximately 14 percent). Reopen any partially closed holes at the leather-hard stage with the needle tool before they dry fully.

rows.problem: Foot ring chips when the trimmed piece is handled
rows.cause: Porcelain bone-dry is fragile and the foot ring edge is the most exposed point
rows.fix: After trimming, bevel the outer edge of the foot ring very slightly with a fingertip while still at leather-hard. This removes the sharp corner that chips most easily.
